extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, historians of mathematics, and mathematicians interested in foundations/axiomatization (graduate students and researchers)
extracted.subtask_short: purity of method analysis in geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing Hilbert's 'purity of method' questions in the foundations of Euclidean geometry: when informal/intuitive assumptions are dispensable or necessary, how axiomatization and model-construction reveal hidden algebraic conditions, and how higher mathematics informs elementary constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity of method / appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'purity of method' concern focuses on a general consideration of 'appropriateness'—whether an assumption used in a proof or construction is appropriate (needed) or dispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on intuitive or informal assessment alone; an assumption that seems inappropriate may be required. Examine the complexity of concepts involved in the assumption and test dispensability via formal/axiomatic analysis (e.g. Hilbert's examples where intuitive assumptions turn out to be necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatization as prerequisite for full investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Full investigation of geometry requires its axiomatization and cutting it loose from its 'natural epistemological roots' so one can study logical relationships between axioms and theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the axioms in play, examine how theorems depend on axioms and the reverse (independence, equivalence), and use axiomatic formulation to reveal hidden assumptions. Treat axiomatization as essential to settle questions about what must be 'adjoined' to obtain Euclidean geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-mathematical results count as geometrical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-geometrical or meta-mathematical investigation is a legitimate source of geometrical knowledge when it alters or informs intuitive geometric content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether abstract/model-theoretic results have direct bearing on intuitive geometry (they may 'effect an alteration in geometrical knowledge'): if so, they should be counted as part of geometrical knowledge rather than dismissed as merely formal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of higher/abstract mathematics to inform intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher mathematics (abstract algebra, ordered field theory, analytic constructions) may be required to resolve questions about elementary constructions and intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to employ non-elementary tools to analyze elementary propositions (e.g. Hilbert's use of Pythagorean vs Euclidean field properties to analyze construction problems). Recognize that elementary statements can contain 'hidden higher-order content'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model construction for independence and counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence investigations involve constructing models (often analytic or algebraic) to show that certain assumptions or properties fail in some models (e.g. Hilbert's countable Pythagorean subfield model where the line-circle or triangle construction fails).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When testing whether an axiom or intuitive assumption is necessary, build explicit models (minimal/countable when helpful) demonstrating the failure; choose branches of mathematics that give fine control over models (analytic geometry, field constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic characterization of constructability (Pythagorean vs Euclidean fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructions justified by Hilbert's Axioms I–V correspond algebraically to the Pythagorean field property; unrestricted straightedge-and-compass constructions correspond to Euclidean fields (fields closed under square roots for non-negative elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine whether a geometric construction is performable in a given axiomatic system, check the algebraic condition on the underlying coordinate field: if the field is Pythagorean then constructions equivalent to ruler + 'segment mover' are possible; if the field is Euclidean (closed under square roots) then full compass constructions are realizable. Use these equivalences to translate geometric constructability questions into field-theoretic ones (e.g. presence/absence of particular square roots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish restricted vs unrestricted compass usage
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an essential difference between allowing the unrestricted use of a pair of compasses and allowing a compass only as a 'segment mover' (Streckenübertrager) for measuring off segments and angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate which constructions are permitted under restricted-compass rules (straightedge + segment mover) versus full compass rules. Hilbert shows some problems solvable with unrestricted compass are not solvable with only a ruler and Streckenübertrager; identify algebraic counterparts (Pythagorean vs Euclidean field properties) to decide permissibility rather than relying on informal intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assuming continuity ad hoc; identify weaker field properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaps in constructability need not always be due to continuity failures; often a weaker algebraic field property (Euclideanness) is the real issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than adding continuity-like axioms (e.g. 'the circle is a closed figure') piecemeal or ad hoc (such as the circle-circle property), investigate whether a weaker, more natural algebraic condition about the coordinate field suffices to guarantee the desired geometric property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix foundational presuppositions (logic and arithmetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by fixing the starting point of the investigation: 'We consider as given the laws of pure logic and full arithmetic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which background mathematical theories (arithmetic, logic, analysis) are presupposed when asking what must be adjoined to obtain geometric theories. This choice affects what can be considered 'elementary' or 'admissible' in subsequent axiomatizations and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study elementary mathematics from an advanced standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary or 'primitive' geometric problems often require a non-elementary point of view to obtain full results; 'elementary mathematics must be studied from an advanced standpoint.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow recourse to more advanced theories (number theory, analysis) when they reveal structure or hidden content in elementary propositions; treat such detours as legitimate and often necessary rather than violations of 'purity'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use minimal/countable Pythagorean subfields for counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Hilbert constructs minimal Pythagorean subfields of the reals (countable) containing particular elements (e.g. 1 and π) to produce models where expected points (e.g. a particular square root) do not exist, yielding counterexamples to certain constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To demonstrate failure of a construction or property, build the smallest field closed under the allowed algebraic operations and show absence of a required element (e.g. sqrt expressions). Minimality arguments can highlight why some constructions aren't guaranteed by the axioms in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical methodological limitation: use familiar branches for model control
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical work in constructing models tends to rely on branches of mathematics that are most familiar and offer the finest control (e.g. analytic geometry, ordered field theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing independence or counterexample constructions, favor mathematical techniques that provide manageable, controllable descriptions of models. Recognize this as a practical constraint rather than a conceptual deficiency.
